question: Can the ordinary test user write to cgroup.kill on one fresh, owned, empty child of its delegated user scope?

method.held_identity_checks: The mount, parent, leaf and control descriptors were retained. The leaf was a strict child below the cgroup mount and the worker scope; the worker and its original supervisor stayed outside the leaf.
method.operational_assumption: Cooperating same-user tasks and administrators leave the fresh probe-owned namespace untouched. This was an operational assumption, not a measured global or adversarial isolation guarantee.

observations.four_leaf_checks: Each observed domain type, empty cgroup.procs and cgroup.threads, populated 0, and zero descendant cgroups.
observations.final_manager_defaults: The unloaded unit's infinity runtime and default stop values were not the active bounds. Active runtime180/stop5/Delegate=yes were checked before the leaf operation.
observations.readable_config: The observed ordinary sudo PAM includes did not contain pam_systemd; the login variant did. sudo.conf contained no active directive. sudoers was unreadable to the ordinary user.
observations.effective_privileged_migration: UNKNOWN: readable files do not establish the effective PAM service, plugin defaults or absence of all migrations.

limits: An empty-leaf write proves access for this ordinary-user setup, not termination of a root-credential process or successful deadline firing.
No sudo, root command, payload, production guard invocation, policy change, runtime reset or daemon was started by this probe.
Continuous containment during sudo policy and PAM phases and survival of a kill-capable supervisor remain unverified. Privileged tests remain withheld.
No performance or competitive result follows. Linux default dispatch remains disabled and issue #2 remains open.
